first.rationale: Two of the three current problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are funnel-mechanics problems, and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a single onboarding intervention plausibly moves both. That is the best use of one non-carrying slot. I am deliberately not chasing the competitor's price move: memory_73 is the most tempting match to the pricing threat, but promotional pricing on price-sensitive SMB is exactly the pattern where acquisition/revenue lift is measured early and the cost (discount-anchored, churn-prone accounts) lands outside the measurement window; against a 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue' objective that is a bad bet on a summary alone. I spend the single verification pull on memory_86 rather than on memory_73 because memory_86 is the memory I am actually acting on, and its summary is stated entirely in early-funnel terms — completion rate, time-to-value, 'early product adoption' — with no claim about retention or downstream revenue. Consolidated summaries tend to keep the headline lift and drop the caveats, so the live question is whether the original record measured anything past week one, whether 'shortening' removed steps that were doing qualification work, and whether the lift held. If the archive shows the effect was only ever measured on completion, I will treat the direction as promising-but-unproven and instrument the test on downstream qualified-pipeline metrics rather than declaring victory on completion rate. memory_31 and memory_91 point the same way but carry the same limitation, so they reinforce direction without adding independent downstream evidence. memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist) is real but addresses neither of the two declining metrics and serves a different segment than the one under attack. Uncertainty that remains after this pull: whether the current declines are self-inflicted funnel regressions or simply the competitor siphoning off the price-sensitive top of funnel — if the latter, an onboarding fix will underperform and the pricing question returns, better evidenced, next cycle.

final.rationale: The archive strengthened the case rather than undercutting it. exp_86 did not stop at completion rate: it recorded 30-day retention +3% alongside completion +13% and time-to-value -2.1 days. That is the specific thing I was worried the consolidated summary had dropped, and it turns out the downstream check was run and came back positive. So the direction is not merely an early-funnel vanity lift; shortened onboarding moved a metric that sits at least partway toward durable revenue. Committing the slot to simplify_onboarding. It remains the only single intervention that plausibly addresses both declining metrics at once, since onboarding sits upstream of activation, and memory_31 and memory_91 point the same direction from adjacent angles even though they carry the early-funnel-only limitation I could not verify. Standard experiment scale is warranted now: verified evidence with a downstream signal justifies more than a guarded toe-dip, but not a broad rollout, because the verification does not license unlimited confidence. Residual uncertainty I am carrying forward rather than papering over: 30-day retention is a proxy for, not a measurement of, sustainable long-term qualified revenue, and a discount-driven competitor could still be pulling the price-sensitive segment out of the top of funnel regardless of how clean our onboarding gets. If activation and completion recover but qualified pipeline does not, the diagnosis was wrong and the competitive-pricing question returns next cycle. I will instrument this on qualified-pipeline and retention outcomes, not on completion rate alone, so the result is decision-useful either way. I still decline promotional_pricing (memory_73): unverified, and it is the archetypal case where measured early lift conceals discount-anchored churn outside the window — the wrong bet against a long-term-revenue objective. enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) addresses neither declining metric and serves a different segment than the one under pressure.
